body.heading: Energy on the move, energy in store
paragraphs: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. Anything moving has it, and it grows quickly: double an object's mass and you double its kinetic energy, but double its speed and the energy quadruples. That is why high-speed crashes are so much more destructive than slow ones, and why braking distances stretch so alarmingly with speed.

Potential energy is energy stored by position or shape, waiting to be released. A boulder on a cliff edge, water behind a dam, a drawn bow and a stretched spring all hold potential energy. Nothing is moving yet — but the arrangement is loaded, and the energy will appear the moment things are let go.

body.heading: The endless swap
paragraphs: Most moving systems are really a conversation between the two forms. A rollercoaster is hauled slowly to the top of the first hill, banking potential energy all the way. Then it falls: potential becomes kinetic, the train screams through the dip, climbs the next rise and trades the energy back — losing a little to friction and air at every exchange.

A pendulum does the same swap twice per swing, all kinetic at the bottom and all potential at each end. A thrown ball trades kinetic for potential on the way up, pauses weightless at the top with the energy fully stored, then spends it all again on the way down.

body.heading: Putting stored energy to work
paragraphs: A hydroelectric dam is potential energy on an industrial scale. Water held high behind the dam falls through pipes, its potential energy becomes the kinetic energy of flowing water, and that spins turbines to generate electricity. The height of the dam matters as much as the amount of water.

Engineers think in these trades constantly: a wind-up toy, a pole-vaulter's bending pole, a bouncing ball. Energy is never created or destroyed in any of them — it just changes form, with friction always skimming a little off into heat.

description: A rollercoaster is an argument between two kinds of energy. Kinetic is motion happening; potential is motion waiting its turn.
